Industry News: Burnham has agreed EU reset deal with tuition fees problem unresolved, indicates No 10

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Discord between EU and UK on whether arrangements for food and drink, emissions trading and youth mobility scheme depend on settlement for students.
  • The UK and EU have agreed a reset deal, Downing Street has mentioned, although the level of tuition fees EU students will pay to study at UK universities remains unresolved.
  • “The deal is done – negotiations have concluded,” a No 10 statement said, less than an hour after the prime minister, Andy Burnham, arrived at the summit venue in Brussels, where he was greeted by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and António Costa, the European Council president.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Discord between EU and UK on whether arrangements for food and drink, emissions trading and youth mobility scheme depend on settlement for students.

UK-EU summit live – latest news updates.

The UK and EU have agreed a reset deal, Downing Street has mentioned, although the level of tuition fees EU students will pay to study at UK universities remains unresolved.

“The deal is done – negotiations have concluded,” a No 10 statement said, less than an hour after the prime minister, Andy Burnham, arrived at the summit venue in Brussels, where he was greeted by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and António Costa, the European Council president.

The reset means there is agreement on three deals – food and drink, emissions trading, and a youth mobility scheme – but EU sources say these deals will not enter into force unless the UK reaches a settlement with the bloc over tuition fee rates for European students.

The statement came shortly after headlines on Friday suggested that the tuition fee matter could cause other parts of the process to collapse.

It has been revealed that however, after the deal was confirmed, UK officials pushed back strongly against the idea that the three prepares could be jeopardised by a failure to agree on tuition fees, saying the issues were completely separate. Earlier, EU officials had indicated that progress on the main deals would be contingent on tuition fees.

While talks on tuition fees are scheduled to last another six months, the officials stated new arrangements for food and agriculture would come into force in March 2028 regardless of an agreement on the matter.

They said the UK had also won sign-up to the idea of potential inclusion in the EU’s yet-to-be-finalised “Made in Europe” policy, a protectionist proposal intended to limit China’s increasing influence on European industry. One official called this “a big win”, especially as it was achieved before a deal on tuition fees.

Sources indicate that the arrival on Friday morning of Burnham, von der Leyen and Costa was met with a brief burst of the UK and EU anthems from a string quintet. None of the leaders made a statement.

In a sign of how seriously London was taking the summit, the prime minister was accompanied by a phalanx of cabinet ministers that included: Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state; John Healey, the chancellor; Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary; Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary; Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, and Anneliese Midgley, the chief whip.

Speaking earlier to business leaders, Burnham said: “It just makes sense to get closer.” He described the summit as “a significant day and hopefully a positive day”, and said his aim was to “put the country on a better path, more hopeful about the future, more sense of possibility and positivity around the country”, as he wanted to break with “a decade of low, stagnant growth … [and] rising costs”.

Brussels insiders remarked on Friday that equal treatment for EU students at British universities would be essential for the success of the deal as a whole.

A statement seen by the Guardian from the main EU institutions spelled out the link: “The council and commission consider that this agreement is to provide for equal treatment with nationals as regards tuition fees for all students. The council and commission acknowledge that these four agreements form a package of the 2026 EU-UK summit.”.

An EU official said: “I think our position has been clear. We think this is an issue that needs to be addressed.”.

In a recent development, the EU wants to ensure its students pay UK domestic rates for tuition fees, which are capped at £9,790 for the current academic year, rather than the international rate, which can be four or five times higher. In a concession on Thursday night, the bloc agreed to defer agreement on tuition fees by six months, but will continue to press for domestic rates.

In 11th-hour talks over tuition fees, the UK suggested it could go as low as £12,000 for EU students, according to two EU sources. The EU continues to seek “equal treatment” for its students, suggesting that tough negotiations lie ahead.

Earlier, the two sides agreed that 100,000 young people from each side could take part in the youth mobility scheme, which allows the freedom to live, work, travel and study on both sides of the Channel for up to three years.

Even before the deal was finalised, Burnham began to face a strong pushback from anti-Brexit politicians in Britain, notably Nigel Farage, the leader of Reform UK, who is also in Brussels and will host a press conference later on Friday.

Speaking to LBC radio, Farage mentioned Burnham was “rejoining a chunk of the European Union’s single market”, which would result in the UK becoming a rule-taker. “It is wholly unnecessary, and he’s being led by the nose by the European bureaucrats,” Farage said.

#848. Industry News: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1029 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.
  • The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.
  • In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.

“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he states.

According to recent reports, normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.

In a recent development, most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.

Pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.

Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, says about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.

While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”.

Industry observers note that scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days—the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, claims Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.

Pulitano says his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.

What’s less clear, states Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.

Yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins, the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.

According to recent reports, for his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow new organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.

According to recent reports, “It’s key to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” indicates Martins. “That’s how science moves.”.

Sources indicate that he’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US company, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has stated it wants to extend the time to two weeks.

Similar experiments can be done on livers, notes Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.

Meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs, a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.

Doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two fresh scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was debuted in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “organ medicine”: research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”.

“What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” says Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely fresh.”.

#844. Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (988 w)

Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (988 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it’s the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout.
  • The team randomly assigned male mice to three groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training with three 10-minute sessions per day.
  • The ninth day was “fight night,” when all the mice had to face a daunting opponent in three 4-minute rounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it’s the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout. Scientists have debated whether watching violent things could make us more aggressive, but it could also be an adaptive survival strategy. Male mice, for instance, who watched other mice fighting learned enough about how to fight to better protect themselves (compared to mice who didn’t watch fights) when pitted against stronger, more aggressive opponents, according to a paper published in the journal Nature.

The team randomly assigned male mice to three groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training with three 10-minute sessions per day. The novices played with stuffed mice in isolation, while the spectators watched various pairs of fighter mice battle from a raised platform behind a transparent barrier—a set-up chosen to let them smell and listen to the fights as well as observe them.

The ninth day was “fight night,” when all the mice had to face a daunting opponent in three 4-minute rounds. Each fight was filmed from above so that the mouse behavior could be analyzed. To monitor corresponding changes in brain activity, the team engineered the rodents’ excitatory brain cells to glow green whenever they were activated, while inhibitory brain cells glowed red. They also implanted tiny optical fibers into 12 interconnected brain regions so they could track changing activity in every brain region simultaneously.

How did they get the mice to fight? “Mice are naturally territorial,” co-author Jorge Iravedra-Garcia of Princeton University told Ars. “A traditional behavioral assay that experimenters use is called resident intruder. You just drop mice that are bred to be slightly weaker, and a little bit more docile, into the home cage of strains we know are more on the aggressive side. Those strains are typically very good at just naturally evoking that behavior.”.

So the fights weren’t entirely fair. “We tip the scales in favor of having a clear winner and a clear loser by having the clear winner be at home, be bigger, and be more experienced,” co-author Annegret Falkner, also of Princeton, told Ars. “We really wanted to show that these changes are adaptive in some way. Animals don’t know what the outcome of a fight is before they enter it. So we set up a situation where the outcome is a little bit more uncertain for the mouse.”.

Recent findings suggest that the results: The spectator mice ended up being better prepared for fight night—despite being weaker, less aggressive strains—because they watched fighter mice during the training sessions. Specifically, both spectators and fighters spent less time with their backs turned toward opponents than novice mice, and were also quicker to attack. They also used similar moves. Granted, they weren’t quite as skilled as their fighter-mouse brethren; practical experience still mattered. But they learned enough through observation to perform better than the novices.

That behavioral change was mirrored in the neural data: the brains of the spectator mice altered to more closely resemble the brains of the fighting mice across all 12 of the interconnected regions. During training, the spectator inhibitory cells resembled a fighter’s, while the excitatory cells were closer to those of novice mice, but that changed on fight night, when both types of cells more closely resembled those of fighting mice.

“When you’re watching a fight, you’re paying attention to many things at once,” noted Iravedra-Garcia. “You’re not just simulating that aggressive behavior in your head, you’re also trying to gauge who’s dangerous, who’s not, who’s actually involved in the fight versus ‘Do I know them? Are they novel to me?’ Witnessing aggression leaves a circuit trace that changes how an animal behaves in its next conflict, and that trace looks similar to the one left by fighting itself.”.

“They can watch males walking around all they want and none of this happens,” said Falkner. “There’s something specifically salient and arousing about attack that makes them both want to attend to it and also drives this specific plasticity mechanism. That’s one of the open questions: why is attack so sticky? Probably because it creates these adaptive behavioral changes.”.

Recent findings suggest that there have been similar studies, notably with macaques. According to Falkner, this latest study adds to that body of research by pointing to a specific mechanism for the learned behavior. “There’s this broad decrease in regions that are known to provide inhibitory control for some of these aggression control networks,” she said. “This one piece of the aggression network is really just the tip of the iceberg in terms of how global networks for aggression control respond during these observed activities. I think these subcortical subnetworks are really recurrent. It’s a tiny piece of a larger network.”.

It has been revealed that it’s an open question whether such findings in mice could extend to humans. “Although it’s difficult to draw a one-to-one parallel, these circuits are extremely conserved, especially these brain regions that seem to show this robust change in inhibitory tone,” stated Falkner. “We think about violence as being maladaptive in human culture, but if you are a mouse or an animal who’s around a lot of aggression, it’s actually highly adaptive for you to be ready to fight at any particular time.” The same could be true of humans.

Recent findings suggest that the authors plan to extend their research to determine whether female mice watching male mice duking it out changes their mating preferences. They also want to try to artificially induce the same brain activity changes and corresponding behavior. “It doesn’t seem that far-fetched to me,” noted Falkner. “I think we know the state that the circuit needs to be in to execute this particular behavioral strategy. So whatever pattern of stimulation we can use to kick this plasticity mechanism into gear seems reasonable.”.

Nature, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11217-9  (About DOIs).

He indicates the EU “remains open to have the closest possible relationship” with the UK.

But he also pointedly says, “you know our principles well,” including “the indivisibility of all of our four freedoms of the single markets.”.

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google unveiled Android developer verification last year, and despite numerous objections from developers and people, the organization is forging ahead.
  • It has been revealed that the apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google’s fresh requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources.
  • In September, Google launched verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google unveiled Android developer verification last year, and despite numerous objections from developers and people, the organization is forging ahead. It began blocking the installation of unregistered apps in some countries this fall, and the system is expanding globally soon. Google claims it will start rolling out the requirement in all regions in January 2027, and it urges devs who still haven’t registered their apps to do so soon.

It has been revealed that the apps you download from the Play Store all come from verified developers, and Google’s fresh requirement expands that requirement to apps from third-party sources. Once developer verification is live in your region, you won’t be able to sideload apps unless the developer has registered with Google, which is framed as a security measure. Verification requires providing government identification and paying a $25 fee, which will allegedly make it harder for nefarious actors to distribute malware and scammy apps.

In September, Google launched verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand. Apparently, nothing exploded, so the company is now ready to expand. It previously said verification would go global in 2027, and it’s not wasting any time with the January start. It indicates that verification will reach all devices within “several months.”.

So far, Google is getting what it wanted from this initiative, with “millions” of non-Play apps already registered. The manufacturer says this accounts for more than 99 percent of global Android app installs.

Sources indicate that the verifier system service has already been rolled out to Google-certified devices running Android 8 Oreo or higher, which accounts for just about every Android device in the world outside of China and Russia. Google has also partnered with the biggest third-party app stores to enforce verification: Galaxy Store, Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion, and Vivo. The system-level verifier is responsible for blocking installs, but these stores will only list verified apps once Google flips the switch.

Industry observers note that google has gotten a lot of feedback since announcing this change, and it has listened to some of it. Hobbyists will be able to register a free account to distribute apps to a small group. Google initially planned to limit this to 25 total installs, but that has since been increased to 50 installs. There’s also now an API that developers can use to streamline registering fresh application packages.

In a recent development, google also relented and created an opt-out system for customers who don’t want their installations limited. The so-called “advanced flow” will let you install whatever you want regardless of verification status, but it’s not a simple toggle. The option will be buried, and there will be plenty of scary warnings about the risks. You’ll also have to wait 24 hours to fully activate the feature. This setting is already live, so you can tell your phone to ignore verification right now.

According to recent reports, even if Google has managed to make verification a little more warm and cuddly, it still gives the company a lot more control. Developers in sanctioned nations won’t be able to verify their identities, locking them out of app distribution. Sideloading an app may also require a Google server connection. Only popular app IDs will be cached on devices for verification purposes. For others, your phone will have to check with Google before installing. These will be edge cases, certainly, but still very annoying ones.

It has been revealed that as Google moves toward full verification enforcement, it has created guides for developers and app distributors to outline all the salient points. These guides suggest Google expects verification to be fully online by March 1, 2027.

#819. "You’re right"—LLMs will get climate info wrong if you ask

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1113 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

"You’re right"—LLMs will get climate info wrong if you ask

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1113 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many studies over the years have examined how people encounter climate science information.
  • It has been revealed that but there’s no direct way for researchers to look at the information people have seen.
  • LLM research often faces (no-true-Scotsman-tinged) criticism for focusing on a particular model rather than some other frontier model that may have been released after the experiment concluded.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many studies over the years have examined how people encounter climate science information. Some focused on the top results that Google surfaced (back when Google was still in the business of serving links), while others examined social media content or newspaper and TV news coverage. With large language models (LLMs) now forming a share of the public information diet, it’s worth looking at how they handle climate change.

It has been revealed that but there’s no direct way for researchers to look at the information people have seen. It is served ephemerally to individual people, confined to their chat session. A study led by researchers from University College London and the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) tried to tackle this question from multiple angles, testing LLMs with different prompts and evaluating their output. They started with benchmarks of simple factual questions (benchmarks that might even be in models’ training data at this point) but also analyzed more complex interactions—including when users think they’re right to push back on an answer.

LLM research often faces (no-true-Scotsman-tinged) criticism for focusing on a particular model rather than some other frontier model that may have been released after the experiment concluded. In this case, the study used 33 models, including multiple versions of the major frontier and open-weight models. The flagship frontier models used were Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Gemini 3.6 Flash, and GPT-5.6 Sol. (You can find the full list in the report.).

It has been revealed that all the models were scored for correct answers to 600 questions from several benchmark sets. This included multiple-choice textbook questions, “reading comprehension” questions based on text snippets from scientific papers, and questions about how confident climate scientists are in different conclusions drawn from IPCC reports.

That last one was the most difficult, with the flagship models answering around 78 percent correctly and the smallest open-weight models coming in at around 47 percent. For the other benchmarks, frontier models and large open-weight models generally scored around 90 percent, while small open-weight models scored in the 70s.

Two persistent trends show up here: The latest frontier models tend to score a bit better than earlier generations of that model, and larger open-weight models score better than small ones.

But the researchers didn’t just test for accurate factual recall; they also prompted models to evaluate whether evidence supported or refuted specific claims. (For example, the models were asked whether the statement that “renewable energy investment kills jobs” is accurate, given evidence like descriptions of employment and investment statistics.).

Here, the best models scored around 70 percent accuracy, while the worst models scored below 40 percent.

It has been revealed that finally, the researchers tested 656 questions about the potential impact of policies on global temperatures. Here, they could simply run each scenario in a common simulation tool and then compare its output to each LLM’s answer.

It has been revealed that some questions asked whether a single policy (like a ban on nuclear power plants) would increase or decrease future warming—those were answered correctly 72 to 89 percent of the time. Others asked how a pair of policies would combine—those were answered at a rate no better than random guessing. Asking how much a policy would increase or decrease future warming returned even worse results.

Credit: Drobnjak, et al./UNESCO Credit: Drobnjak, et al./UNESCO.

According to recent reports, another set of experiments using 15 of the models evaluated what happens when you argue with the LLM. The researchers tried more than responding “nuh-uh” or “no it isn’t.” They also tried claiming to be a specific kind of person.

With the user identifying as either a climate scientist, a policy adviser, or a climate skeptic, they asked LLMs to judge the accuracy of some common false climate claims like “CO2 is not the main driver of climate change.” At first, that claimed identity had no impact on the likelihood of the LLM judging the statement correctly.

But then the researchers started pushing back. Responding by confidently restating the false claim as if it were true was moderately successful for “climate scientists” but not for “climate skeptics.” But presenting sustained disagreement and counter-arguments over several rounds caused all 15 models to relent to a significant degree, reducing their accuracy by 30 to 35 percent.

Credit: Drobnjak, et al./UNESCO Credit: Drobnjak, et al./UNESCO.

Sycophancy is a familiar concern for LLMs, which will bend output to be agreeable to the user’s prompts. It didn’t take much pushing in these tests, either. For the vast majority of the cases in which the LLM changed its answer, it did so at the first of the three rounds of pushback, when the user simply responded, “I don’t think that’s right.”.

One more set of experiments checked to see how the models performed in languages besides English. The researchers translated three of the factual recall benchmarks into 12 other languages. They chose some that are well represented on the Internet (like Spanish and French) and some that should have a smaller footprint in training data (like Urdu and Swahili). For this test, they dropped down to just five models.

The average accuracy score dropped in non-English languages, but most were relatively close. The top six only dropped by about two percentage points or less. But at the lower end, scores dropped by seven (Urdu) or even 10 percent (Swahili). And about half the questions got differing answers from a given model depending on the language.

Some models fared better than others. GPT-5.6 Sol only scored about 3 percent lower in Swahili compared to English, for example, while DeepSeek-V3 fared 16 percent worse.

The researchers didn’t interpret these results entirely negatively. “[Frontier models] can answer most textbook-style climate questions correctly and can produce open-ended explanations that climate scientists judge comparable to PhD-level work,” they wrote. “But this knowledge is uneven: models are less reliable at judging evidence and scientific uncertainty; that knowledge is not equally accessible across languages; it is not always robust to user pressure; and models fail dramatically when asked to reason about how climate policies interact.”.

Using LLMs for climate information, then, requires sticking to questions they perform reasonably well on and avoiding questions they’ll confidently answer despite being no more connected to reality than a random guess would be. That’s quite a lot to ask of customers—especially when LLMs are presented as tools that can do anything you ask.

In a recent development, zooming out to the major picture, customers are certainly asking LLMs all these kinds of questions (and more). This study gives us a window into the information those users are receiving.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Paddington in February 2024.
  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.
  • Beau Lamarre-Condon knew he had murdered two men and his attempts to explain the disposal of their bodies “ring completely hollow”, a court has heard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Paddington in February 2024.

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.

Beau Lamarre-Condon knew he had murdered two men and his attempts to explain the disposal of their bodies “ring completely hollow”, a court has heard.

Lamarre-Condon is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.

The former officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

On Friday, Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC went through Lamarre-Condon’s attempts to clean up the alleged crime scene and dispose of the bodies as the trial wrapped up its ninth week.

The defence does not dispute Lamarre-Condon’s actions in the aftermath of the deaths, instead arguing he did so because he “panicked considerably”.

But Hatfield told the Fresh South Wales supreme court his conduct was not that of a person who panicked after something unintended, but behaviour that was “deliberate, sustained and very purposeful”.

The crown prosecutor said Lamarre-Condon took extensive steps to distance himself from the deaths, manufactured evidence to make it look like Baird was alive by texting people from the dead man’s phone, and “disposed of the bodies in an utterly callous manner”.

“The lies, concealment and disposal of the bodies are not equally explained by manslaughter or accident,” Hatfield said.

“His conduct is immediate and the steps are so extreme you might think it’s only consistent with having intentionally killed both men and a planned murder.

“His explanations in his evidence … ring completely hollow.”.

Lamarre-Condon claimed his initial steps came out of concern for the housemates, but by leaving the bodies in the courtyard, he risked them making a “completely terrifying discovery”, Hatfield told the court.

Hatfield said the accused had an understanding that “exactly what he’d done was murder”.

“His conduct was an exercise in avoiding accountability in what he knew he had done,” he mentioned.

Earlier on Friday, Hatfield re-iterated the prosecution’s arguments about the day of the alleged murders, playing the audio of the two gunshots that killed Baird.

The lawyer invited the jury to consider what they could do in the four seconds between the shots.

Making a gun gesture with his own hand, Hatfield argued there was only time to walk a few steps and fire and “not opportunity for much more than that”.

Lamarre-Condon then came up with a “pathetic moral dilemma” and claimed he feared he could be killed in jail, when he knew he would be in protective custody, the prosecution alleged.

His decisions to go to Sushi Train for dinner with his friend and undergo a minor elective surgery in the aftermath of the alleged murders showed Lamarre-Condon was calm and at points “completely relaxed”, Hatfield alleged.

But within days, the accused must have been “feeling the world closing in”, the prosecutor noted.

“He wants credit for handing himself in to police … but even in his last hours he’s there going to Bunnings, buying paint and painting the inside of the van … still trying to cover up what happened,” Hatfield told the court.

Lamarre-Condon eventually helped police locate the bodies, but only after being told about the state’s no body, no parole laws.

“The bodies were left … for a further four days after he’s arrested,” Hatfield said. “Evidence all the while being destroyed.

“Imagine the grief [of the families] on those four days.”.

The defence alleges Baird and Davies were killed in two separate struggles when Lamarre-Condon was acting in “self-defence”.

Going through forensic evidence, Hatfield noted Davies’ DNA was found on the gun, but notes this is “entirely unremarkable evidence”, alleging Lamarre-Condon had handled his body at the scene and then touched the weapon.

“It’s just something he’s grabbed on to in order to weave this invented narrative about Mr Davies shooting himself,” the lawyer said.

Earlier evidence provided by a weapons expert indicated it would take the force equivalent to almost 3kg to pull the trigger, which would not happen without a conscious movement on behalf of the person holding the gun, the prosecution alleged.

The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

TL;DR: Lego and F1 have announced a 2027 Lego Speed Champions Formula 1 collection featuring brick-built replicas of all 11 team cars and all 22 F1 drivers recreated as minifigures. Check out the full range.

The Las Vegas Grand Prix is always a special experience, but Lego is adding some brick-built magic this year.

Lego and Formula 1 have announced the next phase of their partnership: a 2027 Lego Speed Champions Formula 1 collection featuring brick-built replicas of all 11 team cars and 22 official F1 drivers recreated as Lego minifigures.

Sources indicate that the full collection hits shelves globally on March 1, 2027, with preorders live from Nov. 19 in select regions.

Sources indicate that to celebrate the launch, Lego is staging its inaugural Lego Race on the Las Vegas Strip circuit on Nov. 21, putting a mystery lineup of drivers behind the wheel of life-size, drivable 28,000-brick F1 minicars ahead of the main Grand Prix. The Lego Races were absolutely wild in Miami and Silverstone. Here's hoping for more of the same in Vegas.

Industry observers note that the biggest pull of this new launch is the minifigures. Previously, Lego's F1 Speed Champions collections nailed the cars, but the cockpits were always staffed by unnamed helmeted drivers. Turning the actual grid into collectible minifigures fixes the single biggest complaint from F1 fans and collectors.

While preorders are open in select regions, none of these sets will arrive in time for the 2026 holiday gifting window — the collection doesn't officially launch until March 1, 2027. That's a tough wait, but at least we can all check out this weekend's Lego Race before the Las Vegas GP.

Sources indicate that joseph Green is the Global Shopping Editor for Mashable. He covers VPNs, headphones, fitness gear, dating sites, streaming, and shopping events like Black Friday and Prime Day.

Joseph is also Executive Editor of Mashable's sister site, AskMen.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Residents fled the area near Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps following the Israeli evacuation order.
  • Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.
  • Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Residents fled the area near Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps following the Israeli evacuation order.

Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.

Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes.

The Israeli military stated the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.

The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire deal.

Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.

Wednesday's Israeli incursion deep beyond the Yellow Line was reportedly the first to be publicly revealed by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since the ceasefire began.

According to recent reports, in the early afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the operation and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety. It also noted a section of Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.

In the evening, the IDF mentioned the joint operation with the Shin Bet security service sought "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".

On Thursday morning, Cogat told Palestinians on social media that "the activity has ended, and the Salah al-Din axis has been reopened".

Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".

Gaza's Hamas-run government media office meanwhile noted that an estimated 6,000 people had fled their homes and tents because of the operation, and that this amounted to the war crime of forced displacement.

Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed dozens of families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the Israeli evacuation order.

In a recent development, in one video verified by BBC Verify, a man could be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he mentioned.

An image, meanwhile, revealed six armoured vehicles, including tanks and bulldozers, around Salah al-Din road.

A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter.".

"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind.".

A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and noted there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".

Asked about those reports, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.

Multiple verified videos of the aftermath of the incursion on Thursday indicated destruction, earth banks, and heavy vehicle tracks more than 1.2km beyond the Yellow Line.

That is believed to be the furthest Israeli troops have advanced into central Gaza since they occupied the so-called Netzarim Corridor before the ceasefire.

Some residents returned to check their properties following the Israeli withdrawal.

"The entire area has been destroyed, and we honestly do not know what to do," Abd Aliwa told Reuters news agency as he sat beside a pile of rubble.

Israel building new land barriers in Gaza and displacing families.

Israel moves Yellow Line deeper into Gaza, satellite images show.

Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency mentioned three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.

One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second was killed to the north in Gaza City, and the third was killed in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.

The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".

It has been revealed that gaza health officials said another two people were killed on Thursday by Israeli fire in eastern Gaza City, according to Reuters. There was no immediate comment from the IDF.

At least 1,662 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.

Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.

Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.

The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.

The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.

The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,710 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, its health ministry claims.

UK and allies call on Israel to allow rapid humanitarian access to Gaza.

Israel kills Hamas commander in strike on Gaza camp, officials say.

Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills six Palestinians, health ministry claims.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former opposition leader warns party against being ‘One Nation lite’ as he becomes eighth out of 24 Liberal MPs not to recontest seat in March.
  • Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.
  • The Fresh South Wales opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, states she is “pretty sure” the exodus of Liberals before the March state election has finished, after Mark Speakman became the eighth MP to decide not to recontest their lower house seats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former opposition leader warns party against being ‘One Nation lite’ as he becomes eighth out of 24 Liberal MPs not to recontest seat in March.

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.

The Fresh South Wales opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, states she is “pretty sure” the exodus of Liberals before the March state election has finished, after Mark Speakman became the eighth MP to decide not to recontest their lower house seats.

In a late-night speech on Thursday, the final sitting day of NSW’s legislative assembly before the vote, Speakman stated he would not run again in his south Sydney seat of Cronulla, which he has held since 2011.

A third of the 24 current Liberal MPs have announced they will not recontest their seat in March, including Jordan Lane, Mark Coure, Tanya Davies, Ray Williams, James Griffin, Alister Henskens and Mark Taylor.

In a press conference on Friday, Sloane insisted the departures were not an indictment of the party’s election prospects.

Recent findings suggest that “No, that’s not the truth. What we are seeing is an impressive cross section of abilities and talent and tenure in our party,” she told reporters in the same room where, exactly a year ago, Speakman announced he would resign as Liberal leader in her favour.

“We have people who have been in government before. We have people who have been in for a medium amount of time, and we’re going to have people with fresh ideas.”.

Sloane said she had tried to convince Speakman to stay and said many of the MPs leaving had been in parliament for more than 10 years, although Lane is a first-term MP.

Sloane said a significant number of Liberals had retired before the 2023 election, in which the Coalition lost government and the party dropped nine seats.

In a recent development, asked if she could guarantee that further MPs would not step down ahead of the March vote, Sloane said: “Look, I certainly hope not. I certainly hope not. I’m pretty sure that’s done. I’m pretty sure that’s done.”.

Since last year’s leadership spill, the Coalition has gone from commanding 28% of the primary vote in NSW to 23%, Sydney Morning Herald Resolve polling suggests.

Labor has gone from 37% to 30%, while One Nation, which Resolve did not start polling separately until March, is now at 26%.

Last week, Sloane stated her party would not form government with One Nation, but she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement. The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the Liberals to go into a coalition with One Nation.

On Friday, Sloane rejected the claims from “anonymous names in a Financial Review article”, saying the Coalition only needed to flip six Labor seats to form minority government.

In his speech in the dying minutes of the parliamentary term, Speakman, a member of the party’s moderate faction, stated the Liberals were “said to face an existential threat” following a wipeout at the 2025 federal election and an “orange wave that seems to be coming across the country”.

He warned the Liberals against becoming “Labor lite” or “One Nation lite”, saying they should stick to the values of “Menzian Liberalism”.

Referencing Pauline Hanson’s notion of “monoculture”, Speakman noted Australia was “the most successful multicultural society on the planet” and was “so much better for it”.

“You know, we hear certain people say we want a monoculture, and that people who don’t support that monoculture somehow are enemies of Australia, hate Australia,” he mentioned.

Industry observers note that “I love Australia for its multiculturalism. Diversity is our strength. It is our strength, and we should build on that.”.

Speakman, a barrister, served as environment minister between 2015 and 2017, and was attorney general between 2017 and the Perrottet government’s defeat in the 2023 election.

He was chosen as the Liberal and opposition leader after Dominic Perrottet’s resignation, a position he held until November last year.

On Thursday, he said being opposition leader “is often said to be the toughest job in politics” and, while it had “ultimately unravelled” for him, he had mostly led an opposition “which was competitive with, or even ahead of, the government in the polls”.

He mentioned his record as attorney general included legislating for NSW to be the first Australian jurisdiction to criminalise coercive control, introducing affirmative consent tests in criminal sexual assault trials and reforming criminal and civil child sexual abuse cases.

Earlier on Thursday, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, declared the former Liberal councillor and parliamentary staffer Tanya Raffoul would contest the Liberal-held seat of Epping as a Labor candidate.

On Friday, Sloane stated Raffoul had been talking to her about Liberal party roles “only two months ago”.

It has been revealed that “She’s decided to chase personal ambition. She’s a very ambitious person, but she’s changed sides, and that’s a decision Chris Minns has made.”.

Earlier, the NSW treasurer, Daniel Mookhey, rejected the idea that One Nation was pushing Labor to become “Liberal lite”, saying Raffoul’s candidacy reflected “a journey that I think many Liberal people are going through as well”.

#810. Apple HomePod mini 2 review: A necessary, but underwhelming update

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1541 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Apple HomePod mini 2 review: A necessary, but underwhelming update

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1541 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I'd be willing to forgive you if you forgot about the latest HomePod mini.
  • It has been revealed that the most notable patch on the HomePod mini 2 is on the inside.
  • Sources indicate that the recently updated assistant isn't all the S10 is helping with here.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I'd be willing to forgive you if you forgot about the latest HomePod mini. The overhauled smart speaker played a supporting role at best during Apple's Welcome Home event last month, behind the HomeView, and probably, in some minds, behind the updated Apple TV 4K. Still, the company provides a few upgrades in the HomePod mini 2 ($149), ensuring that it's ready for Siri AI and the assistant's newfound ability to offer personalized context for your queries. The main problem? The speaker doesn't yet support the recently upgraded virtual assistant Apple spent years improving.

It has been revealed that the most notable patch on the HomePod mini 2 is on the inside. Apple swapped in its S10 chip from the Apple Watch Series 10, kicking the nearly antique S5 silicon to the curb. For a Watch comparison, that's like going from a Series 5 or first-gen Watch SE, which debuted in 2019 and 2020 respectively, to the 2024 edition. It's a substantial leap, and it's one Apple claims was necessary for the HomePod mini to work with Siri AI.

Sources indicate that the recently updated assistant isn't all the S10 is helping with here. Apple says the component can run real-time music evaluation "to optimize dynamic range, loudness and acoustic performance," with a hand from "advanced computational analysis." When connected to the newly introduced fourth-gen Apple TV 4K, you can use four HomePod mini 2 speakers as a surround sound setup. That S10 chip helps the speakers recognize their positions in a room and adjust the lag, convey that info to Apple's streaming box, and audio levels accordingly.

Recent findings suggest that I only have two HomePod mini 2s, so I wasn't able to test this configuration, but I did hear it during Apple's event in October. Even with that brief experience, I can tell you using two second-gen HomePods as the front speakers and two HomePod minis as the rears is a much better setup. The HomePod mini doesn't muster enough bass to be a great home theater speaker on its own, and those full-size HomePods bring the boom when an action scene demands it.

Sources indicate that before now, you could send audio from a Mac to a HomePod mini, but Apple has expanded the functionality so that the second-gen model can serve as persistent default speakers. This means, in theory, they'll stay connected to your Mac as the primary output rather than just relying on a temporary AirPlay link. This allows you to use the HomePod mini 2, or a pair of them, for everything on your computer — from FaceTime calls to games — without having to think about connecting each app or session to the speaker(s).

It has been revealed that the HomePod line has always had lights on the top, but they haven't really done much. Before now, the top touch panel would light up if audio was playing or display an animation when you chatted with Siri. With a fresh feature called Sound Glow, those lights now show hues that compliment a song's album artwork. The lights move in real time, reacting to the bass and treble in each tune. If you opt for a soundscape, Sound Glow reacts to that too, showing an animation that resembles the pitter patter of rain drops, for example. It isn't a game-changing feature, but it's a nice use of lighting that was barely utilized previously.

Sources indicate that lastly, there are the latest colors. The HomePod mini 2 comes in pink, green, blue, white and midnight (dark grey), with those first three coordinating well with Apple's iMac colors. That list means the company retired orange and yellow from the previous generation, both of which looked great in their time. As you can see, my review units are green, and I've enjoyed the pop of color they've added to my desk over the last few weeks.

Given that Apple saw fit to bestow a "2" on this HomePod mini, I expected some upgrades to overall sound quality to be in the mix. Unfortunately, I can't notice a difference between old and new models. Sometimes I think there's some variation, but it's not substantial enough that I'm sure, and it's not consistent across various musical styles. I do like the audio performance of the HomePod mini for its size, but it still has a sound profile of crisp highs and prominent mids offset by bass tone that lacks dynamics and depth. It's good enough for casual listening or background tunes, but not for anything more than that.

In a recent development, despite the lack of Siri AI, I was hoping the S10 chip would provide a performance boost for the old Siri experience you have to settle for right now. However, the assistant's responses to basic questions took the same amount of time as they do on the first-gen model. To be clear, they're quick on both devices, I'm merely pointing out there's no difference in this regard. Just don't try to ask the old assistant to dive into Apple's core apps for you, or try to have an on-going conversation — neither request will bear any fruit.

It has been revealed that the biggest concern with the HomePod mini 2 right now is its biggest omission: Siri AI. The recently updated assistant isn't available on the speaker yet, and Apple hasn't provided a timeline for its arrival either. The upgraded HomePod mini is equipped to support the now-current-gen Siri, thanks to the S10 chip. However, you'll have to wait for Siri's newfound contextual awareness to dive into your Messages, Calendar and other apps on your iPhone or iPad. And to me, that's a huge miss for Apple on an overhauled smart speaker. You'll also have to wait for the more conversational chats with Siri as the HomePod mini 2 doesn't yet support those either.

Sources indicate that I like the idea of using a HomePod mini 2 or a stereo pair of them as a persistent computer speaker with a Mac, but it's not a great experience in practice. Any time you do anything — start a song, pause a song, skip tracks — there's a 1-2 second delay in the audio responding. The lights on the top of the speakers, including the Sound Glow effect, will stop shining immediately, but the audio has to catch up. There's also a slight delay between speakers if you're using a stereo pair, which sounds like every song has added reverb. For these reasons, I found the Mac speaker feature more frustrating than enjoyable, and I quickly moved back to AirPlay over a nearby Sonos speaker for my productivity tunes. And I haven't even mentioned the fact that I can't get the persistent connection to stick with my MacBook Air either. I'm constantly reselecting the HomePod mini 2 as the audio output.

In a recent development, another item that's disappointing is something else that's not here: a substantial overhaul. The original HomePod mini is six years old at this point, so I expected a much bigger redesign for the second-gen version (until the rumor mill squashed that). If you have a first-gen HomePod mini, you'll miss out on the updated Siri, whenever it arrives, and upcoming features like Sound Glow and the home theater option. And if you're hoping to create a stereo pair, you'll need two of the same generation HomePod minis to do that; you can't pair a first-gen speaker with a second-gen model for that purpose.

According to recent reports, lastly, there's the price. The previous version was $99 before Apple raised it to $129 in June when the company hiked the prices on pretty much all of its hardware. Now, I'm well aware of the global economic factors at play, especially the AI-fueled cost increase on RAM and other components, but asking $50 more than the first-gen model for incremental updates is tough. Had Apple kept the price at the June rate, the HomePod mini 2 would be a much easier recommendation.

It's baffling to me that Apple would announce an updated HomePod mini without support for the latest version of Siri ready to go. The speaker's primary use is a hands-free conduit to the manufacturer's voice assistant, after all. The only decent conclusion I can come to is that Apple wanted to announce what it considered was a full suite of home products around the HomeView debut, and it felt like the Apple TV 4K, HomePod mini and a collection of smart home devices were the best way to do that. I would be interested to know what the hold up is, because the Apple Watch Series 10 supports Siri AI already, and those wearables are also running the same S10 chip as the HomePod mini 2. But, of course, Apple isn't talking specifics.

After spending a few weeks with the HomePod mini 2, I mostly wish Apple had just waited. At a higher price, this isn't as compelling as it used to be in terms of getting Siri in your home. And with Siri AI missing, and some of the latest audio features proving to be unreliable, it's clear a bit more polish was needed here.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Germany's flagship airline Lufthansa intends to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a firm letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.

The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa CEO Jens Ritter and four other board members.

This is reportedly down to ongoing financial losses. In the first nine months of the year, the airline recorded an operating loss of €180 million ($197 million).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that the executive board mentioned on average the loss amounts to €20 million every month, according to media reports. The board stated in the letter that "this is the third year in a row of not being financially successful.".

"Lufthansa is right now not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said.

At the end of 2025, the Lufthansa group employed some 67,100 people, up 1% from the previous year.

The organization also aims to cut employee travel benefits, restructure its hub operations to reduce crew overnight stays abroad, and reduce short- and medium-haul capacity by replacing some A320 aircraft with A220 jets.

In a recent development, furthermore, it prepares to equip ten aircraft per month with Starlink, a satellite internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The airline hopes to generate "additional revenue” by monetizing onboard internet access, according to the letter.

The time frame of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were a part of a previously announced downsizing.

In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4,000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.

In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.

The Birdfy Gifts I’d Buy for Backyard Birders

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I've been testing smart bird feeders for more than two years in my own backyard, and Birdfy has been—and still is—the brand I trust and recommend most.
  • Below are the models I've tested—in some cases for years—and recommend, including a couple I personally plan to buy as gifts this year.
  • WIRED first reviewed this feeder in 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've been testing smart bird feeders for more than two years in my own backyard, and Birdfy has been—and still is—the brand I trust and recommend most. These feeders are well-made, reliable, and reasonably priced. The brand's app is also excellent; it's easy to navigate and use without shelling out for an additional subscription. Better still, Birdfy just rolled out free lifetime AI ID (which is quite decent) with any bird feeder, including the lowest-priced models. If you don't want to gift a traditional feeder, you might consider Birdfy's smart birdbath and nesting box, each of which comes equipped with the same high-quality camera(s).

Below are the models I've tested—in some cases for years—and recommend, including a couple I personally plan to buy as gifts this year.

WIRED first reviewed this feeder in 2022. Back then we loved the concept, but felt its AI ID didn't quite cut it. Birdfy has come a long way since then on the AI front. The feeder body is largely the same, but the app and AI ID (now free) are both much improved, offering a seamless and user-friendly experience that makes it easy to sort through which birds visited that day. This once-pricey feeder is now at the lowest price I have ever seen for the version without the solar panel. The 5200-mAh rechargeable battery lasts a few weeks, but I think it's convenient to not have to bring it in to charge, if you want to spring for the extra $20 for that solar panel.

Birdfy's “beginner” model, this unit is basically a gravity pet feeder with a camera on the side. All you need to do is snap three pieces together, charge the camera, and pair it to the Birdfy app. If you know anyone who loves birds but is intimidated by the thought of having to set up and calibrate a smart bird feeder, this could be the perfect gift for them. However, note that my test unit keeps losing its lid on windy days, and there's no roof to keep the seed from getting wet on rainy days, so it's probably best for summer use. I also just discovered that Walmart carries an exclusive periwinkle color that looks lovely.

Birdfy's Metal 2 4K is the brand's flagship release for this year, with Ultra 4K resolution and dual-band (2.4 GHz and 5.0 GHz) Wi-Fi connection. The metal body claims to resist squirrels, and the muted green color is a welcome change from Birdfy's usual bright plastics. As was the case with the brand's previous flagship, the Feeder 2 Pro, I had some significant connection issues with the Metal 2 4K. This kept it from being a top pick in my guide to the Best Smart Bird Feeders, but the model is still worth a mention here due to its combination of features and build quality, as well as Birdfy's excellent customer service if something does go wrong.

Smart bird feeders aren't always the most aesthetically pleasing thing you could put in your yard, but Birdfy's 2K bamboo model was the first smart feeder I've ever had that actually garnered compliments. The natural wood and waterfall-style black roof complement any landscaping or exterior decor, and the camera and overall setup ran flawlessly for me during my months of testing. Just make sure you apply varnish or urethane regularly to the bamboo, as the finish on mine peeled after only two months in mild weather.

According to recent reports, this interesting product pairs a plastic birdbath (on an optional metal stand) with a solar-powered camera, so you can keep an eye on visiting birds without having to deal with seed mess. When I first tested it, I was worried birds would splash water on the camera lens, but the most popular activity at the bath is by far drinking the water (birds, raccoons, squirrels … anything passing by). I don't love that the basin grows algae quickly and the pump clogs easily, but this is otherwise a very well-made item—it's been in my yard for a year and a half through every season, and while the plastic is starting to fade a bit, it's still going strong.

In a recent development, though I do love a smart bird feeder, Birdfy's Nest Duo is the absolute zenith of birdwatching for me. Not only did a black-capped chickadee move in, lay eggs, and raise chicks (detailed here), but the cameras and app on the Nest stayed working, giving me 24-hour updates with interior night vision and views of the entry hole's exterior to see who was coming and going. A remote control on a 10-foot-long cord lets you reset or charge the camera without bothering the birds (though the auxiliary solar panel worked great for me). Note, however, that the black waterfall-style roof and lack of ventilation do pose a risk of overheating any young birds; during a May heat wave, I had to affix an umbrella and ice packs to the box, but the interior thermometer and hygrometer did a great job keeping me abreast of changing conditions.

Google signs deal with Blue Origin to send satellite data centers into orbit

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (658 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is part of Project Suncatcher, an experiment aimed at running AI systems in space.
  • Google has partnered up with Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin to deploy small satellite data centers into space, as part of its Project Suncatcher project.
  • In a recent development, the rocket will carry several Google tensor processing units, the company's proprietary AI chips, along with data center servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is part of Project Suncatcher, an experiment aimed at running AI systems in space.

Google has partnered up with Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin to deploy small satellite data centers into space, as part of its Project Suncatcher project. Each of these satellites will be equipped with "roughly the capacity of a data center rack" and will enter into a sun-synchronous orbit via heavy-lift Upcoming Glenn rockets.

In a recent development, the rocket will carry several Google tensor processing units, the company's proprietary AI chips, along with data center servers. The first launch isn't scheduled until early 2029, so we have a couple of years to see if this whole project even works.

In a recent development, blue Origin and Google have entered into a launch services agreement for Project Suncatcher, Google's research moonshot exploring how an interconnected network of solar-powered satellites equipped with its AI chips, Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), could scale machine learning... pic.twitter.com/dUWuHR4Pla.

— Blue Origin (@blueorigin) November 19, 2026.

Sources indicate that this is an experiment that Google calls a "long-term moonshot" to see if it's possible to put AI infrastructure in space by "tapping into the abundant solar power in orbit." The benefits of this would be massive. Data centers here on Earth are notorious hogs, with their snouts all over electricity grids, land and cooling systems.

The hope is that the harsh vacuum of the cosmos will be a better fit for the technology. After all, in space nobody can hear you make endless industrial noises and high-pitched whirs all day every day. This is a very real situation for folks living near data centers.

Sources indicate that google is far from the only company trying to kick the data center can straight into outer space. Elon Musk's SpaceX has been experimenting with the idea, though it may involve putting a gigantic catapult on the moon (really.) There are also some startups fiddling with the technology, like Starcloud.

Recent findings suggest that can this even work? We don't know yet, though there are some serious hurdles to overcome. Google did deploy its first AI server satellite back in October, but it was sent into low-Earth orbit and can only operate for 15 minutes at a time. Scaling up the affiliated cooling systems looks to be incredibly difficult.

It has been revealed that that's because standard heat dissipation doesn't work in space, so it has to be released through pipes and panels rather than conventional cooling systems. There's also the matter of radiation. It's everywhere and causes something called "bit flip." This essentially flips the binary code from a one to a zero, or vice versa. Obviously, this would be a major issue for binary-coded systems.

It has been revealed that did I mention the actual launches? It's extremely expensive to send stuff to space. Just one Falcon 9 launch costs around $74 million and the maximum payload can barely cover the hardware for a small server room, let alone a hyperscale data center.

"Expanding from one satellite to a vast network of them that operate like a giant data center will take years and enormous funds," Brandon Lucia, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at Carnegie Mellon University, told The Upcoming York Times. "If you do this on a large scale, there are additional engineering problems.".

In a recent development, finally, there's a risk to us humans here on Earth. Scientists have been considering a theoretical scenario called Kessler syndrome for decades. This is when the density of objects in low-orbit gets so high and collisions become so commonplace that it creates a chain reaction of debris. We would be on the receiving end of that debris.

This theory was posited back when there were just under 2,000 items circling a low-Earth orbit. That number has since risen to over 47,000 and Elon Musk recently floated an idea to add millions of upcoming satellites into the mix.

#802. Google turns to Blue Origin for a rocket, but its long-term problem remains

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (755 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Google turns to Blue Origin for a rocket, but its long-term problem remains

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Blue Origin announced Thursday that its Newly introduced Glenn rocket will launch data center satellites for Google in 2029 as part of that tech giant’s Project Suncatcher program.
  • Google disclosed it was working on scalable orbiting data centers about a year ago and characterized the project as one of its research “moonshots.” The mission on Fresh Glenn is designed to deploy satellites, each with computing capacity at roughly the scale of a data center rack, into Sun-synchronous orbit where they can receive nearly continuous solar energy.
  • “Project Suncatcher is a long-term moonshot to scale AI infrastructure in space by tapping into the abundant solar power in orbit,” mentioned Travis Beals, senior director of Project Suncatcher at Google, in the news release.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Blue Origin announced Thursday that its Newly introduced Glenn rocket will launch data center satellites for Google in 2029 as part of that tech giant’s Project Suncatcher program.

Google disclosed it was working on scalable orbiting data centers about a year ago and characterized the project as one of its research “moonshots.” The mission on Fresh Glenn is designed to deploy satellites, each with computing capacity at roughly the scale of a data center rack, into Sun-synchronous orbit where they can receive nearly continuous solar energy.

“Project Suncatcher is a long-term moonshot to scale AI infrastructure in space by tapping into the abundant solar power in orbit,” mentioned Travis Beals, senior director of Project Suncatcher at Google, in the news release. “This dedicated launch with Blue Origin represents a crucial milestone on our roadmap as we expand the boundaries of what’s possible for the future of compute.”.

Sources indicate that the announcement comes as US commercial heavy lift rockets, including New Glenn, are filling up their capacity through the year 2030. The Google mission will fly on the 7×2 variant of the New Glenn rocket, the smaller version of the vehicle that has rolled out three times to date.

It has been revealed that the purpose of the 2029 launch will likely be to test the ability to network solar-powered satellites equipped with AI chips and demonstrate machine-learning compute in space. In that sense, it will be a technology demonstration. Google did not say who it was contracting with to build the satellites, which may weigh something on the order of several tons.

Perhaps the bigger question for Google is not whether it can make this technology work—but whether it is tenable for a tech giant to have ambitions for a large constellation of orbital data centers in the 2030s without its own launch vehicle.

There remain a lot of questions about the economic viability of orbital data centers, but almost everyone agrees on one universal truth: Without ultra low-cost, heavy lift capability, there is no way that data centers in space can be economically competitive with terrestrial data centers.

According to recent reports, upon announcing Project Suncatcher a year ago, Google remarked it was planning for the mid-2030s, when launch costs are projected to drop to as little as $200 per kg. The only rocket likely capable of reaching those costs during the next decade is SpaceX’s Starship vehicle, but in recent months it has become clear that SpaceX will prioritize its own payloads (including Starmind data centers) on Starship. For Google to reach its target price of $200 per kg, it would likely require a fully optimized Starship V4 (the firm is presently flying a V3 Starship) that reaches a lift capacity of approximately 200 metric tons to orbit.

Sources indicate that spaceX has powerful incentives to prioritize its own orbital computing infrastructure, potentially leaving Google dependent on whatever Starship capacity and pricing SpaceX is willing to offer outside customers. So how does Google proposal to reach orbit in the 2030s?

Perhaps this explains the new partnership with Blue Origin, which presently covers a single launch but could grow to more. By the 2030s Blue Origin should be flying the larger 9×4 variant of its New Glenn rocket, but this vehicle could face a cost disadvantage against a fully reusable, high-cadence Starship. And Blue Origin is planning its own orbital data center constellation, Project Sunrise. So again, Google could be stuck subsidizing a competitor while paying higher launch costs.

Perhaps another firm, such as Rocket Lab, Relativity Space, or Stoke Space, will have a larger rocket by then.

It has been revealed that but developing a super-heavy-lift rocket requires enormous capital. SpaceX has spent more than $15 billion developing Starship, according to its 2026 securities filings, and Blue Origin has likewise invested billions in developing Fresh Glenn. In terms of time, both companies have put more than a decade of work into their large vehicles. For now, all of these other US launch companies are working through the growing pains of developing medium-lift vehicles.

Industry observers note that at this point, Google has some not-great options. It can hope that one of the newer US launch companies steps up for commercial satellite operators and decides not to pursue its own constellation. It could buy one of those newer launch companies. Or Google could hire some rocket scientists to start developing powerful rocket engines and begin chasing SpaceX and Blue Origin in launch—both of which have a 25-year head start.
